H02.why: Slope of a line from an x-intercept and one more condition; H02 gets the second condition from a vertical shift moving the intercept, so the reasoning differs.
Both pair f with g = f + constant and look at x-intercepts/zeros; ACT item only counts zeros of a quadratic.

H03.why: Two linear savings-type quantities compared over time; H03 asks for a scaled strict inequality with rounding up, not equality.
Least whole number for which one linear expression beats another (strict inequality, round up); H03 adds the 'more than twice' scaling.

H04.why: Linear model from two data points; H04 then perturbs only the rate by 10% before evaluating.
Recovering slope and intercept from two values of a linear function.

H06.why: Slope from a standard-form equation (3x − 4y = 12); H06 is the same algebra placed in context and asked as a rate of change.
Rate-of-change reading from a linear model; H06 hides the rate in standard form with opposite signs.

H07.why: Which quadrant a line avoids; H07 is symbolic, with slope and intercept roles swapped.

H08.why: Two cars, combined distance at a combined rate; H08 has a staggered start and cars moving apart from one point.

H09.why: Line through two given points; another point on it is determined by the slope.
Choose which listed point lies on a line fixed by given points; SAT-030 is through the origin.

H10.why: Tiered per-unit pricing (one rate up to a threshold, another rate after); ACT item evaluates a number, H10 asks for the general expression with the n − 3 adjustment.

H12.why: Vertex position of a parabola with a parameter k; SAT-128 fixes one k, H12 asks for the locus of all vertices.

H13.why: Percent increase over a different time window from an exponential factor; SAT-102 squares a factor, H13 takes a square root of a doubling factor.
Doubling-period growth; ACT item solves for time, H13 converts to a percent per half-period.

H14.why: Reading a function table backward to find an input; H14 adds a shift and subtraction.

H15.why: Maximum value of a model; H15 is rational and found by graphing.

H16.why: Very near template: radical equation √(2x + c) = x + d, asked for the set of all real solutions with one extraneous root. H16 adds a step finding k from a given solution; the rest (squaring, x² − 4x − 5, rejecting −1) is the same routine.
Finding a constant from a given solution.

H17.why: Product of radical conjugates (3 + √2)(3 − √2) is the key computation of H17.

H18.why: Constant in a cubic tied to the count of distinct zeros (double root); SAT-284 asks for c given two distinct zeros, H18 finds k from p(3) then counts.
Counting distinct zeros of a factored polynomial with a repeated factor.

H19.why: Number of real solutions via the discriminant; H19 uses only signs of a and c.
Discriminant condition for two distinct real solutions.

H20.why: Same $2,000 at 5% compounded annually for 3 years context; ACT item runs forward and compares to simple interest, H20 runs backward.
Reverse percent to an original value; H20 does it over three compounding periods.

H21.why: Same template: exponential f and the same function with input shifted by 2; asked for the constant ratio of the two for every x (f(x + 2) is how many times f(x)). H21 only flips the shift sign and asks it as a percent.
Ratio f(x + 3)/f(x) for an exponential, constant for every x; same setup and asked quantity.
Horizontal shift relating two exponentials; SAT-120 asks for the shift instead of the ratio.

H22.why: Equation quadratic in form, solved by substitution then summing solutions; H22's inner expression is linear, and the trap is stopping at u.

H23.why: Conditional probability from a two-way table (preference by group); H23 first recovers a missing cell from a given conditional probability.
Reverse conditional (given a group, probability of a preference) from survey counts.

H24.why: Scaling a sample proportion to a school population.
Interpreting a margin of error as a plausible interval; H24 carries it to a population count.

H26.why: Square-unit conversion m² ↔ cm²; H26 converts a per-area rate together with a mass unit.
Rate unit conversion with two factors.

H27.why: Chord, radius and distance from the center (right triangle with half-chord).
Radius 5/chord 8 triangle from the center; H27 extends to the arc midpoint.

H28.why: Same equation shape x² + y² + ax + by = k with unknown k after completing the square; SAT-022 gives the radius, H28 needs an interior-point inequality.
Constant in a circle equation from its radius.

H29.why: Distance between a point and a circle centered at the origin using center distance minus radius; H29 uses tangent circles (sum of radii).

H30.why: Triangle inequality for possible third sides; H30 has all sides algebraic and finds the binding inequality.

official_sat_mirrors: None judged to closely mirror a specific released official SAT item. H17 (one root 3 + √5, find c) and H07 (sign-swapped line, which quadrant) are common SAT-style formats but not copies of a known released stem.

within_list_cues.why: H20 runs 5% compounding backward 3 years (divide by 1.05³); H21 asks what percent g(x) = f(x − 2) is of f(x), which is the same 'value n periods earlier = divide by factor^n' move (1/1.08²). Seen together, H20's method gives away H21.
Both convert an exponential factor over a changed time window into a percent (2^(1/2) vs 1.08^(−2)); mild method cue, not an answer giveaway.

answer_check_notes: All 30 stated answers recomputed and confirmed (H09 distractor 'true points' (−1, 7), (0, 17/3), (11, −9) also verified on slope −4/3; H10 note: distractor 63n − 84 agrees with the true cost at n = 3 only, which is fine since the stem asks for every n ≥ 3).
